translation:
_Nrug raja girgir thaya, dan sahit jajaman._ (King Nrug turned into a chameleon, together with the patron for whom the charity was given.)

One should not give charity to fraudulent (sakut) Brahmins, mockers, and buffoons. Even though charity was given to a Brahmin, King Nrug still had to go to hell; and even these Brahmins, though they had studied all four Vedas, still had to go to hell. Even though King Nrug performed the office of patron (yajaman) faithfully, he had to become a chameleon along with the one for whom he performed it.

In Lintiyu no. 48, page 123, Revered Yadunathji writes: on deep reflection, the saints kept correcting whatever faults they noticed in themselves. Every body contains the fire of digestion (jatharagni); that fire ought to be offered into the sacrificial fire-pit — intent (bhav) is what matters. So while some people take up giving merely to fill the bellies of themselves and their own wives and children, others give charity for a higher spiritual purpose (paramartha); but if it is done without thought, one becomes liable to punishment for misusing the intelligence given by God. At the edge of a courtyard stands a bird-feeder (parabadi), a lovely thing, into which grain is put out for the birds. But there is an iron ladder with steps leading up to it, and if the grain that is put out is not collected afterward, a dog or a cat can climb up by that same stairway and kill the pigeons that come there to feed. That is something one ought to keep in mind. King Nrug used to give away a hundred thousand cows in charity every day, but because of one single mistake in giving, on one day, he had to become a chameleon.

_Kabir sakut brahman mashkara, tahe na dije dan. O bole kul apano, dakshana sahit jajaman._ (Kabir says: do not give charity to a fraudulent Brahmin or a jester — he drowns his own lineage, and along with him the patron who gave the offering.)

Das Kabirji says: do not give charity to a fraudulent Brahmin or a jester. They themselves drown their own lineage, and they also drown, along with themselves, the patron who gave the charity and the offering.

Nrug's name does not occur in the Bhagavat; a story of this kind is found in the Mahabharat, in the Anushasan Parva, chapter 70. In the Bhagavat this story appears in the tenth canto (Dashamskandh), chapter 64. Register no. 232, page 2289.

_Kabir sakat (kalika) brahman mashkara, tahi na dije dan. Sab kutum (sahit) narake chala(viyu), pichhe dakshana sahit yajaman. ||1|| Sath liya rajaman._ (Kabir says: do not give charity to a fraudulent, Kali-yuga Brahmin or a jester — he goes to hell together with his whole family, taking the patron who gave the offering along with him.)

Das Kabirji says fraudulent Brahmins, the Brahmins of the age of Kali, and jesters should not be given charity. Just as King Nrug was made to suffer, so too these people go to hell taking the giver of the charity along with them.

Budiya

_Kabir brahman mashkara, kare janedaka jor. Lakh chaurasime gaye, parabrahmase tor. ||2||_ (Kabir says: the jesting Brahmin relies on the strength of his sacred thread alone; cut off from the Supreme Being, he passes into the eighty-four lakh forms of life.)

Das Kabirji says: fraudulent Brahmins are given to mockery; they are given to fooling people. Wearing the sacred thread, and on the strength of their Brahmin status alone, they beg for gifts and abandon devotion to Parbrahm Vishnu, and so pass into the eighty-four lakh species of birth.

_Kabir sakat brahman mati milo, vaishnav milu chamar. Ank mal bhare bhari bhatiye, mano mile Gopal. ||3||_ (Kabir says: may I never encounter a fraudulent Brahmin — rather let me meet a cobbler who is a Vaishnav; embrace him with full affection, as though you had met the Lord Himself.)

Das Kabirji says: I wish never to keep company with a fraudulent Brahmin. And even if he be an outcaste (chandal) or a sweeper (bhangi), if he is a devotee of Vishnu, embrace him to your heart with such love as though you had met God Himself.

In commenting on this couplet of Kabir's about giving charity to Brahmins, Revered Yadunathji writes in Lintiyu no. 48, page 123: on deep reflection, whatever faults the saints noticed, they went on correcting them. In every body there is a fire in the form of the fire of digestion; that fire ought to be offered into the sacrificial fire-pit — intent is what matters. So some take up giving merely to fill their own bellies and those of their wives and children, while some give charity for a higher spiritual purpose; but if it is done without thought, one becomes liable to punishment for misusing the intelligence given by God. At the edge of a courtyard stands a bird-feeder, into which grain is put out for the birds — a lovely thing; but there is an iron ladder with steps leading up to it, and if the grain that is put out is not collected afterward, a dog or cat can climb up by it and kill the pigeons that come there. That is something one ought to keep in mind. King Nrug used to give away a hundred thousand cows in charity every day, but because of one mistake, he had to become a chameleon.

Sin is an iron shackle, while merit (punya) is a golden shackle.

_Pipa pap na kiya, to punya kiya so bar. Kisika liya nahi, to diya hajar par._ (Pipaji says: even if you have not committed sin, you have still done merit a hundred times over; even if you have taken nothing from anyone, you have still given a thousand times over.)

Pipaji says: even if you have not committed sin, you have still performed acts of merit a hundred times over; likewise, even if you have taken nothing from anyone, you have still given to someone a thousand times over.

Brahmins tend to be envious of one another, and by quarrelling among themselves they harm their own interests. In register no. 422, page 333, in an article titled "Is This True Caste-Pride, or the Pebbles of One's Reputation?", it is written: you do not know that today's caste-institutions (jnati sanstha) are no longer like the flow of the Ganga, but have become worse even than a gutter — because vegetables at least grow from the water of a gutter, while a caste-institution produces nothing but envy. In ancient times the sages (rishi-munis) established the four varnas. Where have more than eighty-four kinds of Brahmins come to intrude into the Brahmin varna today? If a Brahmin's son drinks liquor, he is still counted a Brahmin — where did this "monopoly contract" come from? One who has a vow (?) against performing the three daily prayers (trikal sandhya), yet has an unbending resolve never to step out of the house without first smoking a bidi — is such a person truly fit to be called a Brahmin? "Brahmano brahmanam shvanavat chhuchhurayate" — when one Brahmin meets another Brahmin, they start snarling at each other like dogs. Such is the fire of envy that constantly burns in their hearts.

_Drashtva yatiryati sadyo vaidyo vaidyam natam natah, yachako yachakam drashtva shvanavad-gurgarayate. ||40||_ (Seeing another ascetic, an ascetic; a physician on seeing a physician; a performer on seeing a performer; and a beggar on seeing a beggar — each at once begins to growl at the other like a dog.)

On seeing another ascetic, an ascetic; a physician on seeing a physician; a performer on seeing a performer; and a beggar on seeing a beggar — each immediately begins to growl like a dog.

_Kayastha karatupa kaka yavanashcha jati bandhanah, chaturtha jati vinashyanti shvano sarpo dvijo gajah._ (The Kayastha, the cock, the crow, and the Muslim — these four communities look after their own interest as a bond of kinship; whereas the dog, the Brahmin, and the elephant destroy the very stock of their own kind.)

The Kayasth (the Nagar clerk-caste), the cock, the crow, and the Muslim — these four communities look after their own self-interest; whereas the dog, the Brahmin, and the elephant themselves root out the very stock of their own kind.

If this is the state of the Brahmins, who stand at the very crown of the varna-system, then what is there to say of anyone else?

_Brahman bhangi ek hai, inaki ek-i jat. Vau kafanaku let hai, o teraime khat._ (The Brahmin and the sweeper are one and the same — they are of one and the same kind. That one takes the shroud from the dead; this one eats at the thirteenth-day feast.)

The Brahmin and the sweeper (bhangi) are truly one; they are of one and the same kind. The sweeper takes the shroud off the corpse, while these Brahmins eat the food offered at the twelfth- and thirteenth-day death rites.

_Kabir kot karam palame katai, jau avai ratti ek nam. Anek jug jo punya karai, nahi nam bina kam._ (Kabir says: crores of karmas are cut away in an instant if even a grain's worth of the Name arises; but even if one performs merit for countless ages, without the Name it is of no use.)

Das Kabirji says: even if you have committed millions of karmas, if you take even the slightest bit of the Lord's Name, those karmas are burned away in an instant. But even if you perform merit for countless ages, it is useless without the Lord's Name.

Under the heading "The Strange Fruit of Charity," in Vishwamangal, year 31, issue 12, page 2, there is a detailed article on King Nrug's charity. It states that the cow which had been given in charity to a Brahmin named Jaimini strayed away and wandered into the king's cowshed; the next day it was mistakenly given away again in charity to another Brahmin named Somsharma. Neither of these two Brahmins was willing either to return the cow or to give it up, and as a result the king had to spend a thousand years as a chameleon living in a well — the well known as the "Nrug-tirth," famous by the name of Krukalash Kund. It relates that Shri Krishna delivered him from that well, and so on. Thus do Brahmins become deserving of censure.

After seeing this Krukalash Kund, Vaishnav Jivandasji went on to Ranchhodji's temple and had darshan there; and at Dwarka, Thakor Gangaram, a servant of Shyamdasji, had built a garden (vadi). His temple, upon entering the fort, is on the left-hand side; in his garden there is a well (kui). Jivandasji Maharaj used to cook daily between that well and the kitchen shed there. He stayed there nine days, and after seeing the divine play (lila) of Dwarka, he came to Dhanore. At that time all the Vaishnavs gathered, and Jivandasji Maharaj told them of the lila of Dwarka, saying that it is the Lord's own abode, and that one should go there — but that one should go together with a group of at least ten Vaishnavs, so as to have the joy of katha, kirtan, and satsang. He said that at the place where Vaishnav Jivandasji used to cook together with us, it would be good if a permanent tulsi-platform (kyaro) were built; "this is what we have resolved in our minds since coming here — so build a permanent tulsi-platform there in Shri Jivandasji's name, and plant tulsi there as an offering of our own service." This is what he said with his own sacred mouth.

Shyamdasji, son of Krishnadasji, wrote the biography (paratari) of Jivandasji Maharaj. In it, from Vishram 13, verse 12 onward, he describes how Jivandasji Maharaj went to Dwarka along with his son and his group. It is related there that on the way to Dwarka they came to a village named Pardi Bajanu, where they found a jambu (blackberry) tree that had dried up, its bark having peeled off as well; Jivandasji gave that jambu tree his blessing, saying, "By the time we return from Dwarka, may you have become green again." In memory of this jambu tree, there is today, at the village of Pardi, a well-known place called "Jambudiyo Ovaro" (the Jambu-tree landing), which recalls Jivanji Maharaj. It is further recorded there that at Dwarka, Jivanji Maharaj had a conversation with Ranchhodji in a dream. Shyamdasji, who was Jivanji's son, had also gone with him to Dwarka and had heard this conversation himself; the explanation Jivanji Maharaj gave of it was that whoever — lame, crippled, or otherwise afflicted — comes to Dwarka with true devotion, to such a one he would grant a human birth once more. Further, Jivanji Maharaj said: "At Puniyad or at Shahpura, your wife has today given birth to a son. What will you give me as the reward for this good news?" Shyamdasji then said: "Our body, mind, wealth, son, household, and even our very self — all of it is yours." And so the son who was born in Shyamdasji's home was accordingly named Dwarkadas — it is thereby established that Dwarkadas was born in Samvat 1726, in the month of Bhadarva or Aso.

|| On the Husband and Wife Sharing One Guru ||

|| The Dispute Over a Husband and Wife Sharing One Guru, and Its Resolution Through Rohidas, Pipa, and Parvati (Sita) ||

Second Question — Second Episode — the second query. In the entire universe a great riddle has arisen: when one guru gives the rosary and the tilak to both a wife and her husband, according to what custom does he give it? Since the male disciples of one and the same guru are counted as brothers to one another, and the female disciples as sisters to one another and to the men, resolving this is a real difficulty. But Samagam shows that this confusion arises only for those who have not understood what true devotion to Vishnu (Vaishnav bhakti) actually is, and who have not grasped the real truth of the matter; regarding this a couplet (sakhi) has been spoken as an explanation.

_Raj pirathathi upanyo, udar rahyo dash mas. Chunchi na chukhi Jivana, nij bhagat Rohidas. ||1||_ (Born of the seed and blood of his parents, he remained in the womb ten months; yet, O Jivan, that intimate devotee of the Lord, Rohidas, did not taste even his mother's breast.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that this child, though born from the seed and blood of his mother and father, and though he had remained ten months in her womb — this intimate devotee of the Lord, Rohidas, because his parents were "nugra" (without a guru), would not take his mother's breast-milk until his parents had made Ramanand their guru.

In the Samagam of Sadguru Jivandasji, support is drawn from the biographies (parachari) written by Anantdas. Anantdas wrote nine biographies in all, and among them the verses forming the basis of the biographies of Rohidas, Pipaji, and Namdevji have been brought into the Samagam. An account of this Anantdas is given in the Hindi Vishwakosh, Volume 1, page 156.

_Anantdas-(1) Bhaktamalke rachayita Nabhadasjike gurubhai Vinodijike shishya Anantdasaka samay unke dwara rachit Namdevki parachaike aadhar par vi. sam. 1645 hai. Unhone Pipaki parachaimein apni guruparamparako Ramanandse arambh mana hai aur uska kram is prakar diya hai — Ramanand-Anantanand-Krishnadas-Agradas-Vinodi-Anantdas. Unhone Kabirdas, Namdev, Pipa, Trilochan, Raidas, (Rankavanka, Dhana bhagat, Angadji, San Sed) jaise santoki parachaiyan likhi hai jinse in santoke jivanki bahutasi mahattvapurna baate jnaat hoti hai aur ve lekhakke lagabhag samakalin honeke karan pramaanke roopmein bhi svikar ki ja sakati hai._ (Anantdas (1): a disciple of Vinodiji, who was the guru-brother of Nabhadasji, the author of the Bhaktamal. On the basis of Anantdas's own biography of Namdev, his period is placed at Samvat 1645. In his biography of Pipa, he traces his own guru-lineage as beginning from Ramanand, giving the order thus: Ramanand–Anantanand–Krishnadas–Agradas–Vinodi–Anantdas. He wrote the biographies of saints such as Kabirdas, Namdev, Pipa, Trilochan, Raidas, [Rankavanka, Dhana Bhagat, Angadji, and San Sed]; from these, many important facts about the lives of these saints become known, and because the writer was roughly their contemporary, these accounts can also be accepted as authoritative.)

Rohidasji was a celibate (brahmachari) disciple in Ramanandji's ashram. A merchant (vaniyo) lived nearby. Ramanand had forbidden taking provisions from that merchant's house, but once, because of heavy rain, Rohidas brought the day's provisions (sidhu) from that very merchant's house. When Ramanandji began to offer the food to the Lord, the Lord did not appear to him in meditation. So he asked where the provisions had come from, and was told they had come from a certain merchant. At this Ramanand cursed him, saying: "Go, take birth in a cobbler's house." So, after being born in a cobbler's house, the child would not nurse at his mother's breast; then Ramanandji heard a voice from the sky (akashvani) telling him: "Because of your curse, show grace upon the child born in a certain cobbler's house." When he came to the child, the child explained that if merely eating the food of a merchant who kept dealings with a cobbler had brought such distress, how much worse would the consequence be of drinking the milk of a cobbler's own house? "How can I take in the food and water of these guru-less (nugra) parents?" So Ramanand gave the teaching of the Ram-mantra and initiated the parents, and only then did the child begin to nurse at his mother's breast. The verses (kadi) of Rohidas's biography written by Anantdas relating to this episode have been presented in the Samagam — these are the verses that come after verse 11 of Vishram 1.

_Aradh rat bhai akashvani, sau Ramanande lai pahichani. ||1|| Chamarake ghar beta jayo, so mero nij jan avatar aayo. ||2|| Hari sab katha kahi samajhai, je pichhe te hoti aai. ||3|| Kripavant hoi diksha deho, balak mast rakhi tum leho. ||4|| Hari marag-ka batavo bhed. ||5|| Tab Ramanande kiya vichara, samajhaya sakal parivara. ||6|| Jo tum bhagat ho re bhai, tihaaro (to hari) balak le jivai. ||7|| Tab chamar uthi lago pai, man mane jo jano so karo gosai. ||8|| Tab Ramanand guru jab kina, mathe hath sabanke dina. ||9|| Mala tilak sabanka pahiraya, pichhala pasan sab daravaya. ||10|| Tab stan pan kare Rohidasa, sabanke manaki pahoti aasa. ||11|| Sabahike man bhaya ullas. Dei badhai baja bajave, gher gher kamini mangal gaave. ||12|| Ghor ghor mangal kalas biraje. Sah kutumb mali anand kina, Ramanande balak dina. ||13||_ (At midnight came a voice from the sky, which Ramanand heard and recognized as the Lord's own: "A son has been born in a cobbler's house — that is my own intimate devotee come again as an incarnation. The Lord told the whole story of what had happened before. Now, in your mercy, give initiation, and take up and preserve this child's life. Show him the secret of the Lord's path." Then Ramanand pondered, and gave understanding to the whole family: "If you become devotees, brother, then this child of yours shall be revived by the Lord." Then the cobbler rose and fell at his feet: "Whatever seems right to your mind, O Master, do that." Then Ramanand made him his disciple, placing his hand upon the heads of them all; he had them all wear the rosary and the tilak, and had all their old, impure vessels thrown out. Then Rohidas took his mother's milk, and the hopes of everyone's hearts were fulfilled. Everyone's heart filled with joy; they gave the good news, played musical instruments, and in every home women sang songs of celebration. In every home the auspicious ceremonial pot was set out. The whole family gathered together in joy, for Ramanand had given them back their child.)

|| Sakhi ||

_Janam sunat Rohidasako, sukh payo bhagavant. Karamake bandhan sab kate, so gaave das Anant. ||1||_ (Hearing of Rohidas's birth, the Lord Himself was pleased, that all the bonds of karma had been cut away — thus sings the devotee Anantdas.)

The child Rohidas had thought that it was better to die than to live in the house of "nugra" (guru-less) parents without devotion to the Lord, and with this thought he would not nurse at his mother's breast. Then, at midnight, Ramanandji heard the voice from the sky, and understanding it, realized that a child had been born in a cobbler's house who was an incarnation of his own intimate devotee. The Lord, through the voice from the sky, told him the story of that devotee's past birth — the very brahmachari whom he had cursed to be born in a cobbler's house — and said: "Be gracious, and by giving initiation to this child and to his parents, show them the path of devotion to the Lord, and save this dying child." Then Ramanand reflected and made the child's family understand: "Brother, if you become devotees, your child can be saved." Then they made Ramanand their guru, and he placed his hand in blessing upon the cobbler's head, gave everyone the rosary and the tilak, and had all the old vessels thrown away. Then Rohidas took his mother's milk. Thus the hopes of everyone's hearts were fulfilled, and everyone rejoiced; the good news was given out, musical instruments were played, and in every home women sang songs of celebration and set up ceremonial pots for the auspicious occasion. The whole family gathered together in joy that Ramanandji had granted them back the life of their child.

Sakhi: hearing of Rohidas's birth, the Lord was pleased that all the bonds of this soul's karma had been cut away; thus does the devotee Anantdas sing the praises of Rohidas, the Lord, and the guru.

_Jato nichakule chapi bhakto bhaktim na vismaret, yatha Raidasabhakto'sau nichajo'pi mahatkritah._ (Even a devotee born in a lowly family does not forget devotion — just as the devotee Raidas, though born in a lowly family, became a great one.)

Even if a devotee is born in a lowly family, he does not forget devotion — just as the devotee Rohidas, though of such a lowly family, became a great devotee.

_Bhakt bij palate nahi, jo guj jaay anant. Unch nich gher avatare, pan aakhar sant na sant._ (The seed-nature of the devotee never changes, even should endless ages pass; he may take birth in a high or a low home, but in the end a saint remains a saint.)

The seed-quality that is the essential nature of a devotee does not change; even if endless ages pass, it does not change. Whether he is born in a high home or a low one, in the end he remains a saint.

_Jaat hamari aatma, parameshvar parivar. Saga hamara sant hai, shir par saraj haar._ (Our caste is that of the soul, God is our family; the saints are our own kin, and above our heads is the garland of the Creator's protection.)

Our caste is that of the soul (atma), and God is our family; the saints are our kin and relations; and thus God, our Creator, keeps the responsibility for our care upon His own head.

_Kabir sara kapada ek hai, bich padi hai bhat. Uncha nicha sab ek hai, sab saike jat._ (Kabir says: the whole cloth is of one and the same kind — only the pattern woven into it differs. High and low are all the same; all are of the one kind made by the Lord.)

Das Kabirji says: the whole cloth of the body is of one and the same kind; it is only the pattern printed into it that differs. Thus, whether high or low, all are made of one and the same kind — all fashioned equally by God.

_Kabir Parabrahmake anshaka, upana sab sansar. Purusha to bhai sabe, bahan bhai sabe naar._ (Kabir says: this whole world has arisen from a portion of the Supreme Being; thus all men are brothers, and all women are sisters.)

Das Kabirji says: this whole world has been formed from a portion (amsha) of God; thus all men are brothers, and all women are sisters.

_Parameshvarke petaka, jnani sab sansar. Purusha to bhai sabe, bahan bhai sabe naar._ (Jnaniji says: this whole world has come out of the inner being of God; thus all men are brothers, and all women are sisters.)

Jnaniji Maharaj says: this whole world has been born from the inner womb of God, and so all men are brothers, and all women are sisters.

_Sab jivaka mata pita, kare sakal pratipal. Jnani dekha nayan bhari, naam khara Gopal._ (He is the mother and father of every living being, and looks after them all; Jnaniji has seen this with his own eyes filled with the vision — his true name is Gopal, the protector of all.)

In the Samarthai anga, Jnaniji says: He who is the mother and father of all living beings looks after and nurtures all of them. Jnaniji has directly experienced this truth himself, and so it is fitting that the true name of God, He who sustains all, is "Gopal."

_Ko mehri ko mavadi, kahe beti ko ben. Ek roop sab jivana, pan jude jude ben. ||3||_ (One woman is someone's wife, another is a mother; one is called a daughter, another a sister — all souls are of one and the same form, yet each stands in a different relation.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: among women, one woman may be someone's mother, while that same [kind of] woman may be someone else's daughter, or again someone's sister. Thus it is one and the same kind of woman, yet her relationship differs according to different attributes.

So, as regards the matter of Rohidas, the essence of it is this: in the matter of devotion to Vishnu, Ramanandji became the one guru of both husband and wife; and since Rohidasji took his mother's milk only after this, there is, on that account, no ground at all for raising the objection that a husband and wife sharing one guru implies a brother-sister relationship between fellow disciples — because it is by renouncing every kind of sensual desire that devotion to the guru and the chosen deity (Ishta) becomes fruitful. Now hear the story of Pipaji. Pipaji and Sitaji had one and the same guru, Ramanandji Gosai. From Vishram 8 of Pipaji's biography, the following passage (vachak) is given.

|| Chaupai ||

_Aise bachan sune jab kana, tab rani man manh pichhatana. Kaun paap ham kino mai, bhar joban dukh dino rai. Ab ghar kaise jau gosai, kai tan tyagu kai rakho sharanai. Tab swami bole samajhai, Pipa tumahi bech hi khai. Kai kahu fakiraku dei, bohor tumara nam na lehi. Hasi hasi mudiya daihai gari, tab manmein dukh pavo bhari. Aur santanaki panihari kahi hai, mathe bhar kashthaka ghar hai. Charan seva aru asan jharave, juthan dehai patravari nakhave. Bohor kamini kahai akulani, ham to sikh tumhari mani. Jaise kahiyo taise ham rahiyo, aagya met panv na dharahi. Tab Ramanande kamar magi, tab sundari dekh pichhori bhagi. Manjh phar mekhari kini, ek ekak pehran dini. Kamarin phari madhi mekhala, pahirin nagar kot. Pahile Pipaku pahirai, puni jethai ardhari bolai. Jo sang chalo to pahiro nari, aabhushan sab dharo utari. Sundari kahai na aisi hoi, aur kaho ham karhe soi. Sabate lauthi (Lahori) Sita rani, so chali aai auran mani. Sitako man dekho sacho, swami kahai nagan hoi nachu. Aabhushan sab dharyo utari, dekhe dur aagiyaro nari. Kari pranam bachan liyo ur dhari, manmein aur kachh na vichari. Dar chir bhai jab nagi, lajja chhand deh-the bhagi. Sagharo (sakal) nagar tamaso dekhe, Sita tinahi trin ur lekhe. Rup dekhi Rambha jaiso, mochhe varani na jaa taiso. Kari dandavat charan jab pariya, tab Ramanande mathe kar dhariya. Hirade lagai pritsu bheti, swami kahai dharamki beti. Sab santanaku pranam jab kinha, ank mal de aasan dinha. Kabir Raidas kiya vichara, ghan mata tera avatara. Lok ved bandhyo sansara, so tohe totat na lagi vara. Sansar sukh sab jutha jana, harike charan kamal man mana. Aisi bhagati kaun pe hoi, tan man sahit laj sab(kho)soi. Shurakidhar bin jhujhanka marag aisa hoi, siraku khel sab koi. Lok ved kul paksh bhakt ja karahi, anek janam ghar ke ehi vidh nistarahi. Kabir Raidase kahai samajhai, Sitaki bhakti hamare hoy na aai. Kahyo hamaro mano Pipa, Sitako tum leho samipa. Gangaranko chhodo raju, yate hoy tumharo kaju. Pipa kahai kaha le kije, mere karya na aur hi dije. Ladke ved sab karahi bhandi, swami sang na lije randi. Abhi kahat hai aachhe aachhe, swami laj maroge pachhe. Jo ham kahave sikh tumharo, avagun gun hi bhagat hamaro. Chhal bal kari dahkave nari, inaki prit jnanamein dari. Rajake ghar rani hoi, jogike ghar jogan soi. Suranar mohe inake rupa, bisare bhagati parai grah kupa. Inaki gat mat swami jano, tum aage main kaha bakhanu. Sita kahi maru sir phori, ajahu daad na dehai mori. Tum hi kalank na lau swami, apani chuk maru teh thami. Dasi dur na kije swami, suno ho jagat guru antarjami._ (When she heard these words, the queen repented in her heart: "What sin have we committed, mother, that we are given such grief in the full bloom of our youth? How can I now go home, O Master? Either let me give up this body, or keep me in your shelter." Then the Master spoke to her plainly: "Pipa, he will only sell you off, or hand you over to some faqir, and after that will pay no heed to you at all. Shaven ascetics will mock and abuse you, and your heart will suffer greatly. You will be called the water-carrier of the saints, carrying loads of firewood on your head; you will have to wash the saints' feet and spread out their seats, eat their leftovers, and throw away their leaf-plates." At this the women grew anxious and said: "We have accepted your teaching; as you tell us, so we shall remain — we will not set foot outside your command." Then Ramanand asked for a coarse blanket; seeing this, the beautiful women fled in their veils. He tore it down the middle to make waistbands, and gave one to each. From the torn blanket he made loin-cloths, which they wore throughout the town-fort. First he had Pipa put his on, then he called for the eldest queen. "If you would come along, wear this, woman, and take off all your ornaments." The beautiful queen said, "This we cannot do — tell us anything else, and we shall do it." Of all the queens, Sita, the queen of Lahore, alone, heeding no one, came forward without hesitation. Seeing that Sita's heart was truly sincere, the Master said, "Then dance naked." She took off all her ornaments — the other women stood watching from a distance. She bowed in reverence and took his word to heart, with no other thought in her mind. As soon as her garment fell away and she stood bare, she cast off all shame and ran forth. The whole town watched this spectacle, yet Sita counted it all as but a blade of grass. Her beauty was like that of the celestial nymph Rambha — it cannot be described by me. When she fell in prostration at his feet, Ramanand placed his hand upon her head; he drew her to his heart and embraced her with love, and the Master said, "You are my daughter in the faith." When she had made her bow to all the saints, they gave her the rosary and a seat beside them. Kabir and Raidas then reflected: "Blessed is the mother who bore you, blessed is your birth — the bonds that bind the world by custom and by scripture, you have broken through without the slightest delay. You have known all worldly pleasure to be false, and your mind has come to rest at the lotus feet of the Lord. Who else could attain such devotion, casting away all shame along with body and mind? This is the path of the truly heroic, who fight without holding back — it is a game played by staking one's very head, and not everyone is capable of it. Those who practise devotion bound by custom, scripture, and family loyalty, deliver themselves only after passing through many, many births in this manner." Kabir and Raidas said further, explaining: "A devotion such as Sita's has not even come to us. Pipa, heed what we say: take Sita along with you near yourself. You have already given up the kingdom of Gangaran-garh — through this too your welfare shall be secured." Pipa replied: "What would I do by taking her along? Do not assign me any other task besides my own." "Children and scriptures alike will make a mockery of you, if you do not take a woman along with you, Master." [The queens/onlookers say:] "Right now you speak so very finely, but afterward, Master, you will die of shame." "If I am to be called your disciple, then whatever fault or virtue I have, I am still your devotee. Women beguile through deceit and craft, and their love has ensnared even the wise; she who is a queen in a king's house becomes a female ascetic in a yogi's house — gods and men alike are enchanted by their beauty, forgetting devotion and falling into the well of household life. Their true nature, O Master, you do not know; what more can I explain to you than this?" Sita then said: "I would rather smash my head and die; even now you give me no answer. I will not let blame fall upon you, Master — if I make any mistake of my own, I shall die on the spot for it. Do not cast this servant away from you, O Master; hear me, O Guru of the world, who knows all hearts.")

|| Sakhi ||

_Ber ber binati kare, Sita samre santa. Pativrata sache dhare, so gaade das Anant. Puran._ (Again and again Sita made her entreaty, calling the saints to mind; truly she held to the vow of a chaste and devoted wife — thus sings the devotee Anantdas. Complete.)

When Pipaji was about to set out with his guru Ramanand, the queens, wishing to go along, pressed him with their entreaties; to dissuade them he explained that if they came with him they would have to bear hunger, thirst, and every kind of hardship, so it would be better for them to stay at home. Hearing these words, the queen began to repent in her heart, thinking: "Alas, mother, what sin have we committed that such suffering has come upon us in the very bloom of our youth? O renunciant, how can we now go back home? Either we shall give up our bodies, or you must keep us in your shelter." At this Swami Ramanandji spoke to persuade her, saying that this Pipaji would sell her off, or give her away to some faqir, and afterward would pay her no further attention; that shaven-headed ascetics would mock her and hurl abuse at her, and her heart would then suffer greatly; that he would make her the water-carrier of the saints, make her carry loads of firewood on her head, make her serve at their feet and spread out their seats, feed her their leftovers, and make her throw away the used leaf-plates. At this the women, growing anxious, said that they had already accepted his teaching, and so would remain exactly as he told them to, without ever disobeying his command. Then Ramanand asked for a rough blanket, and, in full view of all the women, tore it up. Tearing it down the middle, he made waist-bands and loincloths out of it and gave one to each of them. He tore the blanket into pieces to make the waist-cloths, and they wore them throughout the town. First it was given to Pipaji to wear; then he called for his eldest queen and said that if she wished to come along she should wear this and take off all her jewellery. The women said that they could not do such a thing, but that they would do whatever else he asked. Of all the women, it was the queen Sita of Lahore who, without heeding anyone's dissuasion, did not stay back — she came forward. Seeing the sincerity in Sita's heart, Swami Ramanand told her to dance while naked, casting off all her ornaments. This whole scene was watched from a distance by the other, hesitant women. Sita bowed in reverence and took his command to heart, letting no other thought enter her mind; and when she took off her garment and stood naked, she ran forward, casting off all shame together with the garment. The whole town watched this spectacle, but Sita counted it all as no more than a blade of straw; her beauty was as lovely as the celestial nymph Rambha's — such that I cannot describe it. When she fell in prostration and touched his feet, Ramanand placed his hand upon her head, drew her to his heart, and embraced her with love, saying: "You are my daughter in the faith." When she had bowed to all the saints, they seated her in their midst and gave her a place beside them. Kabir and Rohidas then began to reflect: "Blessed is your mother, blessed is your very birth. This world is bound by the constraints of worldly custom and scriptural convention, yet you took no time at all to break free of them. You have recognized all worldly happiness as false, and your mind has become fixed upon the Lord's lotus feet. Who else could attain such devotion, that casts away all shame together with body and mind? This is what is called heroic devotion — the path of one who fights without regard for his own life. Everyone else plays it safe, guarding their own life; they practise devotion only according to worldly custom, scriptural convention, and family loyalty, and even after passing through many births, it is only by this weak measure that they attain any deliverance." Kabir and Rohidas went on to say, explaining further: "A devotion such as Sita's is not even to be found in us. O sinner [Pipa], heed what we say, and take Sita along with you. You have already given up the kingdom of Gangarod-garh, and for this reason your welfare will surely follow." Pipaji said: "What use would it be to take her along? It will not let me carry out my own work of devotion — this is not my task; give me some other task instead." "Both children and the scriptures alike will mock you, O Master, if you do not take a woman along with you." "Right now you speak so very finely, but afterward, O Swami Ramanandji, you will die of shame." "If I am indeed to be called your disciple, then whatever good or bad qualities I have, I shall still be called your devotee. A woman deceives through cunning and beguiling craft; her love has ensnared even the wise. She becomes a queen in a king's house, and a female ascetic in a yogi's house; gods and men alike become infatuated by her beauty, and forgetting devotion, fall into the well of the household life. Her true nature, O Master, you do not know — how then can I describe it before you?" Sita then said: "Now I shall smash my head and die, since even now you give me no hearing. O Master, I will not let any blame fall upon you; if I should ever make a mistake of my own, I shall die then and there for it. Do not cast this devotee-servant far away from you, O Master; hear me, O indwelling Guru of the world."

Sakhi: Sitaji, calling the saints to mind, made her entreaty again and again; she truly held to the vow of a devoted and chaste wife — thus does Anantdas sing her praises.

_Bhaktasya purvapunyena jaya bhaktimati bhavet, Pipa bhaktapriya Sita yatha tadanugaa'bhavat._ (By the merit of a devotee's past lives, he obtains a wife full of devotion; just as Sita, the beloved wife of the devotee Pipa, became one who followed after him in devotion.)

By virtue of a devotee's past merit, he obtains a devoted wife; just as Sita, the beloved wife of the devotee Pipa, became one who followed after her husband in his devotion.

Jagdish no. 46, page 98.

|| Kavit ||

_Pipa pratap jag basana, naharako updesh dio. Pratham Bhavani bhakt mukti maganiku dhao, satya kaho tehi shakti. So dradh Hari sharan bataayo, Ramanand pad payau bhae ati bhaktiki sivaan. Guru asankhya niramol, sant dhari rakhat griva, paras paranali sarasa bhai. Sakal vishva mangal kio. Pipa pratap jag basana, bahiraku updesh dio._ (Such was Pipa's worldly renown — that a teaching was given even to the lion-hearted one. At first he ran after the goddess Bhavani in devotion, striving to beg from her the boon of liberation; truly, tell me, that was the power [he sought]. Then he was shown the firm refuge of Hari, and having attained the feet of Ramanand, he arrived at the very furthest shore of devotion. Countless and priceless are the gurus, but the saints keep his memory ever alive around their necks; the touchstone-like tradition [of devotion] became sweeter still. He brought about the good of the whole world. Such was Pipa's worldly renown — that a teaching was given even to the deaf [i.e. the spiritually unhearing].)

Such is the greatness of Pipa, a man of worldly desire, that Ramanand gave his teaching even to this lion-like devotee. At first Pipa strove to attain liberation through devotion to the goddess Bhavani, and it was then that the goddess Shakti herself showed him the true path of the saints — pointing him toward steadfast, single-minded devotion to Hari. Having attained the feet of Ramanandji, he became, apart from devotion to the goddess, a devotee of the very highest devotion to Hari. The guru accomplished a great work: the saints have kept the Lord's Name enshrined in their own throats, and by thus turning him away from the worship of the goddess (Bhavani), he fashioned a beautiful new tradition — a lovely way — of devotion to the Lord, and so brought about the good of the whole world. This worldly-minded Pipa, who had been turned away from devotion, was given the teaching of devotion — so says Pipaji.
